title: Does Every Gram Cost the Same?

scenes.visual: Title card 'Does Every Gram Cost the Same?' over a small and a large dog outline. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP: skin GOLD, heat ORANGE, pumped fluid RED, oxygen BLUE; silhouettes charcoal. Exponent lines: b = 1 GREY dashed, b = 3/4 TEAL solid, b = 2/3 PURPLE solid. Every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: A human is more than two thousand times heavier than a mouse. Does the human burn two thousand times as much energy every day?
scenes.visual: A tiny mouse silhouette on one pan of a balance, a human silhouette on the other; the balance slams down, label 'mass x 2,333'. An ORANGE flame beside each, the human's with a question mark.
scenes.narration: A human is more than two thousand times heavier than a mouse. Does the human burn two thousand times as much energy every day?

scenes.tts: The first film showed why a thick, busy body pumps blood and air. That flow has to deliver whatever the tissue burns. So how much does a body burn?
scenes.visual: Brief replay: the first film's mouse cross-section with RED channels carrying BLUE dots. The RED stream feeds a small ORANGE flame in the tissue, label 'supply must match use'.
scenes.narration: The first film showed why a thick, busy body pumps blood and air. That flow has to deliver whatever the tissue burns. So how much does a body burn?

scenes.tts: In 1883, Max Rubner asked a simple question. Does every gram of an animal cost the same to run? He studied resting dogs of many sizes.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Max Rubner, 1883'. A row of dog outlines from small to large lies resting; each gets an ORANGE heat bar above it.
scenes.narration: In 1883, Max Rubner asked a simple question. Does every gram of an animal cost the same to run? He studied resting dogs of many sizes.

scenes.tts: Dogs suit the question well. One species spans a wide range of sizes. So size can change without changing the kind of animal.
scenes.visual: The dog row stretches: smallest at left, largest at right, a mass axis appears under them labelled 'body mass'. Outlines are one dog shape, scaled, labelled 'same-shape model, not the actual dogs'.
scenes.narration: Dogs suit the question well. One species spans a wide range of sizes. So size can change without changing the kind of animal.

scenes.tts: Take one dog that is ten times heavier than another. If every gram cost the same, it would make ten times the heat. Does it?
scenes.visual: Two dogs highlighted, labelled 'M' and '10 M'. The big dog's ORANGE heat bar has a dashed outline reaching '10 x', with a question card.
scenes.narration: Take one dog that is ten times heavier than another. If every gram cost the same, it would make ten times the heat. Does it?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: No. Total heat rose with size, but much less steeply than mass. Each kilogram of a small dog made more heat than each kilogram of a big one.
scenes.visual: The big dog's ORANGE bar fills only part way, well short of the dashed '10 x' outline. A second panel shows heat per kilogram: the small dog's bar is clearly taller.
scenes.narration: No. Total heat rose with size, but much less steeply than mass. Each kilogram of a small dog made more heat than each kilogram of a big one.

scenes.tts: Then Rubner divided each dog's heat by its estimated body surface. The values came out roughly equal. Heat tracked surface more closely than mass.
scenes.visual: Each dog's GOLD skin outline glows; heat-per-surface bars appear and line up at roughly the same height, label 'heat per unit of estimated surface: roughly constant (a pattern, not proof of cause)'.
scenes.narration: Then Rubner divided each dog's heat by its estimated body surface. The values came out roughly equal. Heat tracked surface more closely than mass.

scenes.tts: In 1932, Max Kleiber gathered resting rates for animals from rats to steers. He plotted them on logarithmic axes, where a power law becomes a straight line.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Max Kleiber, 1932'. Points labelled 'rat' to 'steer' drop onto log-log axes, 'log mass' and 'log metabolic rate', and settle near a straight line (schematic points).
scenes.narration: In 1932, Max Kleiber gathered resting rates for animals from rats to steers. He plotted them on logarithmic axes, where a power law becomes a straight line.

scenes.tts: Metabolic rate equals a constant, called a, times body mass raised to a power, called b. On these axes, b is the slope of the line.
scenes.visual: The equation 'metabolic rate = a × M^b' writes itself above the plot. The line's slope is marked with a small triangle labelled 'slope = b'.
scenes.narration: Metabolic rate equals a constant, called a, times body mass raised to a power, called b. On these axes, b is the slope of the line.

scenes.tts: If b were one, every kilogram would cost the same. Kleiber's line had a slope near three quarters. Rubner's surface rule implies two thirds.
scenes.visual: Three illustrative lines with the same coefficient a pivot through a common point labelled 'same a; slopes compared only': GREY dashed 'b = 1', TEAL 'b = 3/4', PURPLE 'b = 2/3' (computed lines, not the fitted lines of Rubner or Kleiber).
scenes.narration: If b were one, every kilogram would cost the same. Kleiber's line had a slope near three quarters. Rubner's surface rule implies two thirds.

scenes.tts: Now place a mouse and a human on the widely used three-quarter fit. The human burns far more in total, but only a few hundred times more.
scenes.visual: On the TEAL line, a mouse marker '30 g: ≈ 5 kcal per day' and a human marker '70 kg: ≈ 1,690 kcal per day'. A bracket between them reads 'total x ≈ 336' (computed from 70 × M^0.75).
scenes.narration: Now place a mouse and a human on the widely used three-quarter fit. The human burns far more in total, but only a few hundred times more.

scenes.tts: Divide each by body mass. Each kilogram of mouse burns about seven times as much as each kilogram of human. That is a fitted prediction, not a single measurement.
scenes.visual: Per-kilogram bars: mouse '≈ 168 kcal per kg per day', human '≈ 24'; the mouse bar towers, label 'about 7 x' (computed, on the fit).
scenes.narration: Divide each by body mass. Each kilogram of mouse burns about seven times as much as each kilogram of human. That is a fitted prediction, not a single measurement.

scenes.tts: In most comparisons of adult mammals and birds, b is positive but below one. So total rate rises more slowly than mass, and rate per kilogram falls as mass rises.
scenes.visual: The GREY 'b = 1' line fades back; the TEAL and PURPLE lines stay. A falling per-kilogram curve appears in an inset, label 'rate per kg falls as mass rises'.
scenes.narration: In most comparisons of adult mammals and birds, b is positive but below one. So total rate rises more slowly than mass, and rate per kilogram falls as mass rises.

scenes.tts: Treat three quarters as a fit, not a law. The exponent changes with the animals, their state and the method. Its cause is still debated.
scenes.visual: Several schematic fitted slopes fan out, some shallower than PURPLE 'b = 2/3' and some steeper than TEAL 'b = 3/4', labelled 'examples, not bounds'; caption 'a fit, not a law'. Small tags float past: 'which animals', 'rest or exercise', 'which method'.
scenes.narration: Treat three quarters as a fit, not a law. The exponent changes with the animals, their state and the method. Its cause is still debated.

scenes.tts: So across most adult mammals and birds, bigger animals burn more in total. But they burn less per kilogram.
scenes.visual: Recap: the dogs' heat bars, Kleiber's line, and the mouse-human per-kilogram bars side by side.
scenes.narration: So across most adult mammals and birds, bigger animals burn more in total. But they burn less per kilogram.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'Adult mammals and birds: bigger burns more in total, less per kilogram.'
